title: Provide risk-based primary emergency care/first aid in the workplace

lessons.title: Principles of primary emergency care and preparedness
lessons.html:
Important

This content supports, but does not replace, practical training. You must complete hands-on training and assessment with an accredited first aid training provider before acting as a workplace first aider.

Principles

Primary emergency care aims to:

  • Preserve life: keep the airway open, support breathing and circulation, stop serious bleeding.
  • Prevent the condition getting worse.
  • Promote recovery and get the casualty to medical care.

A first aider works within their training. Do what you were trained to do, ask for consent from a conscious casualty, protect their dignity and privacy, and keep information confidential.

Risk-based preparedness

"Risk-based" means first aid is planned around the hazards of your workplace. On a farm these include tractor roll-overs, PTO and machinery injuries, chainsaw cuts, chemical poisoning and splashes, animal kicks and gorings, snake bites, falls from ladders and trailers, heat illness, burns in workshops and kitchens, and drowning in dams.

Being prepared

  • Know where first aid boxes are, check them regularly and restock after use. The General Safety Regulations under the OHS Act require first aid boxes and trained first aiders at workplaces with more than a set number of employees.
  • Add items for your risks: large trauma dressings for chainsaw work, eye-wash for chemical stores, a barrier device for rescue breaths.
  • Know the emergency numbers: 10177 for ambulance and 112 from a cell phone, plus local private ambulance and the nearest hospital. Display them, with the farm's address and GPS coordinates.
  • Plan how to reach remote camps and lands, and where an ambulance can meet you.
  • Keep a list of first aiders and their shifts.
  • Have safety data sheets for chemicals available.

Protecting yourself

Use gloves and a CPR barrier device for every casualty. Wash hands afterwards. If you have contact with blood through broken skin or eyes, report it and seek medical advice the same day.

lessons.title: Scene assessment and life support for all ages
lessons.html:
Managing the scene

  1. Stop and look for danger: machinery running, electricity, chemicals, fire, animals, traffic, unstable loads.
  2. Make it safe if you can: switch off engines and power, keep bystanders back. Never become a second casualty.
  3. Find out how many casualties there are and what happened (the mechanism of injury, for example a fall from a height or a tractor roll-over).
  4. Call for help early, giving location, what happened, number of casualties and their condition.

Primary assessment: DRSABC

Check Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing (look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds), then CPR if not breathing normally. Gasping is not normal breathing.

CPR

CasualtyCompressions
AdultCentre of chest, two hands, about 5 to 6 cm deep
Child (about 1 year to puberty)Centre of chest, one or two hands, about one third of chest depth (about 5 cm)
Infant (under 1 year)Centre of chest just below the nipple line, two fingers, about one third of chest depth (about 4 cm)
  • Rate: 100 to 120 compressions a minute; let the chest recoil fully.
  • Give rescue breaths in the ratio taught on your accredited course (30 compressions to 2 breaths is common for adults). For children and infants, breathing problems are the usual cause of arrest, so rescue breaths are especially important; your course will teach the sequence.
  • If you cannot or will not give breaths, give continuous compressions.
  • Use an AED as soon as one arrives and follow its prompts. Many AEDs have child pads or a child setting.

Choking

  • Adult or child: encourage coughing; if ineffective, up to 5 back blows then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, repeat.
  • Infant: up to 5 back blows with the infant face-down along your forearm, then up to 5 chest thrusts with two fingers. Never use abdominal thrusts on an infant.
  • If the casualty becomes unresponsive, start CPR.

Breathing casualties who are unresponsive go in the recovery position unless a spinal injury is suspected; then keep the head in line and monitor the airway.

lessons.title: Shock, secondary assessment and records
lessons.html:
Shock

Shock is a life-threatening condition in which not enough blood and oxygen reach the body's organs. Causes include severe bleeding (outside or inside the body), serious burns, severe vomiting and diarrhoea, heart problems, severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) and spinal injury.

Signs

  • Pale, cold, clammy skin; grey or blue lips.
  • Fast, weak pulse and fast, shallow breathing.
  • Thirst, nausea, anxiety, confusion, then drowsiness.

Management

  • Call for an ambulance urgently.
  • Treat the cause, for example firm pressure on bleeding.
  • Lay the casualty down. Raising the legs may help if there is no leg, hip or spine injury, as taught on your course.
  • Keep them warm with a blanket; loosen tight clothing.
  • Give nothing by mouth. Reassure them and monitor breathing and response.
  • For anaphylaxis, help the person use their own adrenaline auto-injector if they have one.

Secondary assessment

Once life threats are managed, check the casualty from head to toe. Ask what happened, about pain, allergies, medicines and medical history. Look and feel gently for bleeding, swelling, deformity and tenderness.

Common workplace treatments

  • Wounds: direct pressure, dressing and bandage. For an embedded object, do not remove it; pad around it.
  • Fractures: support in the position found; immobilise with padding and slings.
  • Burns: cool with running water for at least 20 minutes; cover loosely.
  • Chemical exposure: remove contaminated clothing with gloves, flush skin or eyes with plenty of water, check the label and safety data sheet, and call the poison information service or a doctor.
  • Heat stroke: confusion and hot skin are an emergency. Cool rapidly and call an ambulance.
  • Seizures: protect from injury; do not restrain or put anything in the mouth; recovery position afterwards.

Records

Record the incident: date, time, place, casualty details, what happened, findings, care given, who took over and when. Record first aid box use for restocking. The employer uses records for incident reporting and investigation, and reportable incidents must go to the Department of Employment and Labour. Keep records confidential.

Key points

  • Plan first aid around your workplace's real risks and keep kits stocked.
  • Make the scene safe and call for help early.
  • Know CPR differences for adults, children and infants; use an AED as soon as possible.
  • Recognise and manage shock; give nothing by mouth.
  • Record every incident; hands-on accredited training is required.

quiz.question: What does risk-based first aid mean?

options.text: Only doctors can give first aid
First aid is given only after an audit
First aid is only for risky workers
First aid is planned around the hazards of the workplace

quiz.question: How should compressions be given to an infant?

options.text: With two hands as hard as possible
With two fingers, about one third of chest depth

quiz.question: Which is a sign of shock?

options.text: Pale, cold, clammy skin with a fast, weak pulse
Warm pink skin and slow pulse

quiz.question: How should an object embedded in a wound be managed?

options.text: Leave it in and pad around it

quiz.question: Which should never be used on a choking infant?
A casualty in shock should be given water to drink.
Gasping is not normal breathing, and CPR should be started.
